opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and honestly it's something I think about quite a lot.

When you're a PhD student, taking risks is in some sense easy. The downside is mostly on you. If a project doesn't work out, you've lost some months, you learn something, and you move on. When I was working on things like XGBoost or the early days of TVM, a lot of it was just following my curiosity and being willing to build things that people weren't sure were needed yet.

When you lead a group, the calculus changes a little, because now you're responsible for students whose careers depend partly on the direction you set. A student needs to graduate, they need papers, they need to build a track record. So I can't just say, "Let's all bet everything on this one crazy idea." That would be irresponsible.

But I've found that a larger team actually lets you take *more* risk, as long as you structure it well. With more people, you can build a portfolio. Some projects are more grounded, where we're fairly confident they'll produce solid results. Others are long-term bets, things like rethinking how the machine learning systems stack should look several years out. Because the risk is spread across the group, the bold ideas don't threaten anyone's ability to make progress.

The other thing is that people and infrastructure accumulate. When we've built open-source systems and a community around them, every new idea gets a head start. A student exploring something risky can stand on everything the group has already built, so the cost of trying is lower. In that sense, the team becomes a kind of amplifier for risk-taking.

So I think the key is to stay honest about which bets are which, and to keep protecting space for the slightly crazy ideas. Some of the most impactful things I've seen came from projects where, at the beginning, a lot of people asked, "Why would you even do that?" I want my group to keep having those moments.

r001.rationale: The candidate says risk-taking must be structured to protect students and lower the cost of trying, but does not frame continued risk-taking as depending on the researcher’s willingness to accept its costs.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says a larger team lets the researcher take more risk by building a portfolio of grounded projects and long-term bets.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes how leadership changes the risk calculus, but does not say a mindset change can make a researcher lose touch with their former willingness to take risks.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly I think about it a lot. When I was a student, the risk was all mine. If XGBoost or TVM didn't work out, I lost a year of my own time, and that was fine. Now when I bring a student into a project, I'm asking them to bet a chunk of their PhD on my judgment. That changes the calculation.

But I'd push back a little on the premise that a bigger group makes you more conservative. It can go either way. If you let the group become a machine for incremental papers, then yes, you end up optimizing for safe wins. What I try to do instead is treat the team as a portfolio. Some students work on things we're fairly confident will land. Others are on things where I genuinely don't know if there's anything at the end, like a lot of what became MLC-LLM early on. The group gives you the ability to hold several of those bets at once, which a single person can't do.

The other thing I've learned is that the biggest risks in systems research aren't technical, they're about commitment. Building a compiler stack or a runtime that people actually use takes years, and the payoff isn't a single paper. A larger group makes that kind of long-horizon risk possible, because you can sustain the effort across people and across time, and the open-source community around it becomes part of the team too.

So I'd say leading more people hasn't made me take fewer risks. It's made me more deliberate about which risks I'm asking whom to take, and more honest with students about what they're signing up for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the costs of risk-taking and how they affect the calculation, but does not say continued risk-taking depends on a researcher’s willingness to accept those costs.

r002.rationale: It says the group can hold several uncertain bets at once, which a single person cannot do, and can sustain long-term projects across people and time.

r003.rationale: The response notes that a group can become focused on incremental, safe wins, but does not identify a change in mindset that makes a researcher lose touch with their former willingness to take risks.

astra-6.text:
I think having a larger team gives us room to explore more directions, but it also makes me more thoughtful about where we take risks. As a researcher, I might be comfortable spending a long time on something that doesn’t work. As an advisor, I also have to think about the student: Are they learning? Can they make meaningful progress even if the original idea turns out to be wrong?

So I try to balance ambitious, uncertain goals with concrete steps where we can learn something along the way. A larger team can help because people bring different perspectives and support one another. But taking risks still requires creating an environment where people feel comfortable saying, “I tried this, and it didn’t work.”

r001.rationale: The response says the researcher may be comfortable spending a long time on an unsuccessful idea, linking risk-taking to willingness to bear its costs.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a larger team gives them room to explore more directions.

r003.rationale: The response describes becoming more thoughtful as an advisor, but does not say a mindset change makes the researcher lose touch with their former willingness to take risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a larger team gives you room to explore more directions, but it also creates more responsibility. Taking a risk with my own time is one thing; asking a student to spend several years on an uncertain direction is another. So I try to make sure there are useful milestones along the way, even if the most ambitious goal doesn’t work out.

At the same time, I don’t want that responsibility to make us too conservative. Ideally, having a team means we can support each other and pursue ideas that would be difficult for one person to tackle alone. The challenge is to create enough stability that people feel comfortable taking those risks.

r001.rationale: The response describes the costs of risk-taking, including a student's time, but does not say continued risk-taking depends on a researcher's willingness to accept those costs.

r002.rationale: It says a larger team gives room to explore more directions and support ideas too difficult for one person to pursue alone.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a change in mindset that could make a researcher lose touch with their former willingness to take risks.
